LESSON 74 OF 106·Social Engineering and the Human Factor

Pretexting, Baiting and Tailgating

The three classic social techniques that need no link and no attachment: the invented scenario, the offered gift and the held door — and the control that answers each.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Not every social engineering attack involves a message. Some involve a person walking in, being helpful, or simply following the crowd through a door they should not have opened.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A pretext is a story that explains why the person is asking, and it works when the story fits the situation.
  • Physical pretexts work in a specific place, so a delivery uniform in a loading bay is more effective than in an ordinary public area.
  • Baiting leaves something appealing in a place the target will go, turning the target own behaviour into the delivery.
  • Tailgating needs no deception at all; it relies on someone holding a door and not wanting to make a scene.
  • All three succeed because the socially correct action and the secure action are different, and the secure one is awkward.

The background

  • Physical access was the original boundary, and it was guarded by a person at a desk.
  • Access control badges and mantraps replaced the person, which raised the bar for entry.
  • Organisations moved to self-service and contactless entry, which removed the human checkpoint entirely.
  • Physical attacks returned as a targeting mechanism once technical entry was hardened, especially against high-value premises.

Real-world examples

  • An unverified contractor walking through a secure area is a routine and largely unreported event.
  • A USB drive left in a car park is a low-technology, low-cost and still effective route into an organisation.
  • Someone carrying an awkward load through a door is accepted without anyone deciding to accept them.

What to look for

  • Check what your reception process actually does when someone has no appointment, no badge, or no host.
  • Check whether delivery and contractor entry is separated from general visitor entry.
  • Check whether anyone challenges an unknown person without needing permission from a manager first.
  • Check whether there is a defined procedure for a suspicious item found on the premises.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Reducing data exfiltration by malicious insiders

Reading how a national authority separates deliberate insider abuse from staff who take insecure shortcuts because a policy blocks their actual work

Open NCSC resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Make badge-only access the rule, and train staff to challenge rather than to accommodate.
  • Require escorts for anyone without a business reason to be in the area, including maintenance.
  • Issue a short, specific procedure for visitors with no appointment, so the decision is not improvised.
  • Train staff that holding a door is not a security decision they are expected to make alone.
  • Report anything left or found, since a baited device is only a threat once someone picks it up.
